UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE OVERPAYMENT AND FRAUD — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS OVERPAYMENT AND FRAUD INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's statutory framework for unemployment insurance benefit overpayments — what happens after the Employment Development Department (EDD) determines that Jordan Lee was paid more in unemployment compensation benefits than the law allowed. Jordan Lee received an overpayment determination from the EDD dated October 1, 2026, EDD case number EDD-1234567, concerning benefits previously paid on a claim related to Jordan Lee's employment with Acme, Inc., in the amount of $1,200. This document states facts about the statutory distinction between a non-fraud and a fraudulent overpayment, the conditions under which repayment of a non-fraud overpayment may be waived, the specific penalties a fraud finding carries, the notice and appeal rights that attach to an overpayment determination, and the methods California law gives the EDD to recover an overpayment. It does not itself constitute an appeal filed with the EDD, an administrative law judge, or the California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board (CUIAB); it does not determine that Jordan Lee's overpayment is or is not due to fraud; and it does not determine that any waiver applies to Jordan Lee's specific overpayment.

THE STATUTORY DISTINCTION BETWEEN A NON-FRAUD AND A FRAUDULENT OVERPAYMENT
California's Unemployment Insurance Code treats an overpayment of benefits as a single general category — any person overpaid any amount of benefits is liable for the amount overpaid unless a statutory exception applies — but a separate statute carves fraud out as a distinct, more narrowly defined category within that whole. A fraudulent overpayment exists only where the director finds that the individual was overpaid because he or she willfully, for the purpose of obtaining unemployment compensation benefits, either made a false statement or representation with actual knowledge of its falsity, or withheld a material fact. Everything else — an overpayment that was not due to fraud, misrepresentation, or willful nondisclosure on the recipient's part — falls instead into the non-fraud category that the general liability statute expressly distinguishes from fraud, misrepresentation, and willful nondisclosure. The consequences that follow this classification are not symmetric: a non-fraud overpayment can, as described in the clause below, be waived entirely under specific conditions, while a finding of fraud triggers a mandatory monetary penalty, a distinct disqualification period, and, potentially, criminal exposure, described in the clauses that follow.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Any person who is overpaid any amount of benefits under this part is liable for the amount overpaid unless any of the following is applicable: (a) (1) The overpayment was not due to fraud, misrepresentation or willful nondisclosure on the part of the recipient, and (2) the overpayment was received without fault on the part of the recipient, and its recovery would be against equity and good conscience."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1375 (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1375.)
  "If the director finds that an individual has been overpaid unemployment compensation benefits because he or she willfully, for the purpose of obtaining unemployment compensation benefits, either made a false statement or representation, with actual knowledge of the falsity thereof, or withheld a material fact"
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1375.1 (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1375.1.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statutes (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1375, for the general liability rule and its non-fraud language, and § 1375.1, for the specific fraud-finding standard), used as real evidence that California's overpayment scheme is built around a binary fraud/non-fraud classification with different statutory consequences on each side — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular overpayment, and not a determination that any specific claimant's own overpayment is, or is not, due to fraud. These are two independent statutory sections, not subsections of a single section. The quoted language from § 1375 is the identical opening-sentence-and-subdivision-(a) text this corpus's existing Unemployment Insurance Appeal — Information Sheet document already cites, in its own uiappeal_continued_benefits clause, for the related but distinct point that an overpaid claimant is liable for the overpayment subject to a waiver; that overlap is disclosed here rather than presented as new independent corroboration of § 1375(a) itself. The specific waiver conditions that attach to a non-fraud finding, and the specific penalty, disqualification, and recovery consequences that attach to a fraud finding, are new research not previously cited anywhere in this corpus, and are addressed in the clauses that follow. This document does not itself find, or advise any specific claimant regarding, whether any specific overpayment is due to fraud.

WAIVER OF REPAYMENT FOR A NON-FRAUD OVERPAYMENT
The same statute that makes an overpaid claimant generally liable for the amount overpaid sets out three separate, independent grounds on which that liability can be waived. The first, described in the clause above, applies where the overpayment was not due to fraud, misrepresentation, or willful nondisclosure, was received without fault on the recipient's part, and recovering it would be against equity and good conscience — a three-part, conjunctive standard, so all three elements must be met, not merely one. The statute provides two further, independent grounds beyond that equity-and-good-conscience standard. The second applies where the person who received the overpayment cooperates with the department in an investigation that results in the assessment of a penalty against someone else — specifically, a penalty against an employer under a statute addressing employer-induced fraudulent claims, or a prosecution or other penalty action under the general false-statement penalty statute. The third applies where the department itself determines that waiving all or part of the liability is in the interest of justice because the overpayment was a direct result of inducement, solicitation, or coercion by the employer, rather than by the claimant's own conduct.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The person who received the overpayment cooperates with the department in an investigation that results in the assessment of a penalty under Section 1144 or the prosecution or other action taken to impose a penalty pursuant to Section 2121."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1375(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1375.)
  "The department determines that it is in the interest of justice to waive all or part of the liability established under this section because the overpayment was a direct result of inducement, solicitation, or coercion on the part of the employer."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1375(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1375.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1375, subdivisions (b) and (c)), used as real evidence that California's non-fraud waiver standard is not limited to the equity-and-good-conscience test alone, but includes two additional, independently sufficient waiver grounds — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular overpayment, and not a determination that any specific claimant's own overpayment satisfies any of these three grounds. These two quoted passages, subdivisions (b) and (c), come from the same statutory section as each other and as the equity-and-good-conscience ground quoted in the clause above; they are being treated as one source together with that ground, not as independent corroborating sources on separate points, though each subdivision states a substantively distinct, independently sufficient basis for waiver. Subdivision (b)'s cross-references — to a penalty statute addressing employer-induced fraudulent claims, and to a general false-statement penalty-action provision — were checked directly against the statutory text quoted here rather than assumed; this document does not independently verify or restate those cross-referenced provisions' own substance beyond confirming their citation numbers appear correctly in the quoted text. This document does not itself apply for a waiver, and does not determine that any specific overpayment does, or does not, meet any of these three grounds.

THE PENALTY, DISQUALIFICATION, AND CRIMINAL EXPOSURE A FRAUD FINDING CARRIES
A fraud finding under the statute described above carries consequences beyond the underlying repayment obligation itself. First, a mandatory monetary penalty: once the director finds a fraudulent overpayment, the statute requires the director to assess against the individual an amount equal to 30 percent of the overpayment amount — a fixed, non-discretionary percentage added on top of the overpaid benefits themselves, not an alternative to repaying them. Second, a period of disqualification from future benefits: a related statute independently disqualifies an individual who willfully made a false statement or representation, or withheld a material fact, in order to obtain unemployment compensation benefits, and a further statute sets the length of that disqualification at two weeks (running from the week the disqualification determination is served) plus up to 13 further weeks, within a three-year window, for an individual who was not actually paid benefits as a result of the false statement. Third, potential criminal exposure: this corpus's existing Unemployment Insurance Benefits — Claimant Information Sheet document already establishes, and this document does not re-verify independently here, that a willful false statement or material nondisclosure made to obtain benefits is separately punishable under the same code's general false-statement penalty chapter by up to one year in county jail, imprisonment in state prison, a fine of up to $20,000, or both.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "the director shall assess against the individual an amount equal to 30 percent of the overpayment amount"
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1375.1 (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1375.1.)
  "An individual is also disqualified for unemployment compensation benefits if: (a) He or she willfully, for the purpose of obtaining unemployment compensation benefits, either made a false statement or representation, including, but not limited to, using a false name, false social security number, or other false identification, with actual knowledge of the falsity thereof, or withheld a material fact in order to obtain any unemployment compensation benefits under this division."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1257(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1257.)
  "An individual disqualified under subdivision (a) of Section 1257, under a determination transmitted to the individual by the department, and who was not paid any benefit amount as a result of their false statement or representation, is ineligible to receive unemployment compensation benefits for two weeks commencing with the week in which the determination is served upon them, or any subsequent week, for which they are first otherwise in all respects eligible for unemployment compensation benefits and for not more than 13 subsequent weeks for which they are otherwise in all respects eligible for unemployment compensation benefits. No disqualification under this subdivision shall be applied to any week if all or any portion of the week is beyond the three-year period next succeeding the date of the service of the determination. This subdivision shall not apply to an individual convicted under Section 2101."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1260(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1260.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statutes (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1375.1, for the 30-percent monetary penalty; § 1257(a), for the disqualification standard; and § 1260(c), for the length of disqualification where no benefits were actually paid), used as real evidence of the specific, sourced consequences California attaches to a fraud finding beyond the underlying repayment obligation — not a claim about which state's law governs a given overpayment, and not a statement that any specific claimant has been found, or should be found, to have committed fraud. The § 1375.1 quote here is a different passage — the section's penalty-assessment clause — from the definitional passage already quoted in the distinction clause above; the two quotes are non-overlapping substrings of the same section, not independent sources. Section 1257(a) and Section 1260 are different sections from each other and from § 1375.1, not subsections of a single section. This document's drafter confirmed directly that § 1260 also sets a longer, five-week-plus-up-to-10-further-week disqualification, within the same three-year window, for an individual who was actually paid benefits as a result of the false statement (§ 1260(d)); that longer alternative is not separately quoted here to avoid duplicating an already-lengthy citation, but its existence is disclosed so this clause is not read as stating the only possible disqualification length. Section 1260(c) also states that its disqualification 'shall not apply to an individual convicted under Section 2101' — meaning this administrative disqualification and a criminal conviction are not simply cumulative in every case, a nuance this document discloses rather than resolves. The criminal-penalty statement here relies on, and does not independently re-verify beyond, this corpus's own prior verification of Unemployment Insurance Code §§ 2101(a) and 2122 in the existing uiclaimant_false_statement_penalty clause; that reliance is disclosed rather than presented as new independent verification of those two sections. This document does not itself impose any penalty, disqualification, or criminal charge, and does not determine that any of these consequences applies to any specific claimant's overpayment.

NOTICE OF AN OVERPAYMENT DETERMINATION AND THE OVERPAYMENT-SPECIFIC RIGHT TO APPEAL
An overpayment determination is not self-executing; a specific statute requires the director to determine the amount of the overpayment and any fraud-penalty assessment, and to notify the liable person of the basis for that determination. That same statute also times-bar the EDD's own notice in the ordinary case: in the absence of fraud, misrepresentation, or willful nondisclosure, notice of the overpayment determination must be served within the latest of one year after the close of the benefit year in which the overpayment was made, or six months after the date of a backpay award — a deadline that, by its own terms, does not constrain the EDD's timing where fraud, misrepresentation, or willful nondisclosure is involved. Once notice is served, a separate statute gives the person affected — not only the EDD or an employer — the right to appeal to an administrative law judge within 30 days from the date the notice of overpayment was mailed or served, with the director treated as an interested party to that appeal and the administrative law judge empowered to affirm, reverse, modify, or set aside the findings in the notice. This overpayment appeal right is its own, separately numbered statutory provision, not a bare cross-reference to the general benefits-eligibility appeal statute this corpus's existing Unemployment Insurance Appeal — Information Sheet document addresses — though it is structurally parallel to that general appeal right, running the same 30 days and leading to the same further-appeal path to the CUIAB.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The Director of Employment Development shall determine the amount of the overpayment and any assessment authorized under Section 1375.1 and shall notify the liable person of the basis of the overpayment determination. In the absence of fraud, misrepresentation, or willful nondisclosure, notice of the overpayment determination shall be served within the latest of the following periods: (a) Not later than one year after the close of the benefit year in which the overpayment was made. (b) Not later than six months after the date a backpay award was made."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1376 (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1376.)
  "Within 30 days from the date of mailing or serving of the notice of overpayment, the person affected may file an appeal to an administrative law judge. The director shall be an interested party to any such appeal. The administrative law judge, after affording reasonable opportunity for a fair hearing, shall, unless the appeal is withdrawn, affirm, reverse, modify, or set aside the findings set forth in the notice of overpayment."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1377(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1377.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statutes (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1376, for the notice requirement and its timing, and § 1377(a), for the overpayment-specific appeal right and deadline), used as real evidence that California gives overpayment determinations their own dedicated notice-and-appeal statutes, distinct from (though procedurally similar to) the general benefits-determination appeal statute (§ 1328(a)) this corpus's existing Unemployment Insurance Appeal — Information Sheet document already covers — not a claim about which state's law governs a given determination, and not a statement that any appeal from any specific claimant's overpayment determination has been, or should be, filed. These are two independent statutory sections, not subsections of a single section, and neither has been previously cited anywhere else in this corpus. Section 1377(a) itself provides, in language this clause does not separately quote to avoid an overlong citation, that a further appeal from the administrative law judge's decision may be taken to the appeals board under Section 1336 within 30 days, and that both 30-day periods may be extended for good cause defined the same way as in the general appeal statute; this document does not restate that further-appeal mechanic in full here because this corpus's existing appeal document already verifies the materially identical CUIAB further-appeal and judicial-review process, and that overlap is disclosed rather than treated as unaddressed. This document does not itself serve any notice or file any appeal, and does not calculate the actual notice or appeal deadlines applicable to any specific claimant's determination.

HOW CALIFORNIA MAY RECOVER AN OVERPAYMENT
Once an overpayment is established, a specific statute lists what the director may do to recover it, and recovery is not limited to a single mechanism. One option is a civil action against the liable person, which the director may file within one year of the overpayment becoming final in the ordinary case, or within three years where the overpayment involved fraud, misrepresentation, or nondisclosure. A second, separate option lets the director offset the overpaid amount against any future benefits to which the liable person may become entitled, within six years of the date notice of the overpayment determination was served — meaning a claimant who later files a new, otherwise-valid claim can have that new claim's benefits reduced to satisfy an old overpayment, rather than receiving the full new benefit amount in hand. The same statute also authorizes a summary judgment procedure and the ability to reduce or vacate a summary judgment already obtained. Beyond the director's own tools, a further statute directs the state Controller to collect certain overpayment amounts under a general Government Code interagency-intercept collection provision, with amounts collected deposited back into the fund from which the overpayment was made.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The director, subject to this article, may do any or all of the following in the recovery of overpayments of unemployment compensation benefits: (a) File a civil action against the liable person for the recovery of the amount of the overpayment within one year after any of the following, or, in cases where the individual has been overpaid benefits due to fraud, misrepresentation, or nondisclosure as described in Section 1375.1, or where the director has found an overpayment pursuant to Section 1375.7, within three years of any of the following:"
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1379(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1379.)
  "Offset the amount of the overpayment received by the liable person against any amount of benefits to which they may become entitled under this division within six years of the date of the service of the notice of overpayment determination."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1379(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1379.)
  "Amounts collected by the Controller for benefit overpayment accounts, pursuant to Section 12419.2 of the Government Code, shall be deposited in the fund from which the overpayment was made, except that the amounts collected to offset the costs of collections shall be deposited in the Unemployment Administration Fund."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1384 (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1384.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statutes (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1379, for the director's own civil-action, summary-judgment, and offset-against-future-benefits tools, and § 1384, for the Controller's separate intercept-based collection role under Government Code § 12419.2), used as real evidence of the actual, sourced recovery mechanisms California's overpayment statute provides — not a claim about which state's law governs a given overpayment, and not a statement that any specific recovery method has been, or will be, used against any specific claimant. The two § 1379 passages quoted here, subdivisions (a) and (d), come from the same statutory section and are being treated as one source, not independent corroborating sources, though each states a substantively distinct recovery tool (civil action and offset, respectively); § 1384 is an independent, separately numbered section citing a different code (Government Code § 12419.2) for the Controller's own collection role, and is genuinely independent of § 1379. This document's drafter was specifically asked to verify, rather than assume, whether wage garnishment and tax-refund interception are among California's statutory recovery mechanisms for this specific type of overpayment. Having checked § 1379 and § 1384 directly, the honest answer is narrower than that framing suggested: § 1379 does not itself name wage garnishment as a distinct recovery tool (though a civil judgment obtained under its summary-judgment procedure could, once entered, be enforced by the general civil-judgment-enforcement remedies available to any money judgment, a point this document does not independently verify here), and this document did not independently fetch or verify the text of Government Code § 12419.2 itself — it relies only on Unemployment Insurance Code § 1384's own description of that cross-referenced provision as an interagency intercept-style collection mechanism administered by the Controller, without separately confirming § 12419.2's own statutory text against its primary source in this session. This document does not itself take any recovery action, and does not determine which, if any, of these methods applies to any specific claimant's overpayment.

OVERPAYMENT RESPONSE DECLARATION
In connection with the EDD overpayment determination dated October 1, 2026, EDD case number EDD-1234567, concerning benefits previously paid on the unemployment insurance claim between Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc., in the amount of $1,200: Jordan Lee states that, in response to this determination, Jordan Lee intends to take the following action: requesting a waiver of repayment. This declaration records Jordan Lee's stated intention as of the date signed below. It is not itself a request for waiver, an appeal, or any other filing with the EDD, an administrative law judge, or the CUIAB, and it does not determine that any waiver applies or that any appeal, if filed, would succeed. Any waiver request or appeal concerning this determination must be filed directly with the EDD using its own required forms and procedures, within the deadlines described elsewhere in this information sheet.

SIGNATURE AND CERTIFICATION
Jordan Lee certifies that the statements made in this document are true and correct to the best of Jordan Lee's knowledge, and that this document is informational only. It does not itself constitute a waiver request, an appeal, a repayment agreement, or any other filing with the EDD, an administrative law judge, or the CUIAB, and Jordan Lee understands that any such filing must be made directly with the EDD using its own required forms and procedures.

EDD case number: EDD-1234567

Signature: _______________________ Date: _______________

Printed name: _______________________

expectedJSON.body: An overpayment determination is not self-executing; a specific statute requires the director to determine the amount of the overpayment and any fraud-penalty assessment, and to notify the liable person of the basis for that determination. That same statute also times-bar the EDD's own notice in the ordinary case: in the absence of fraud, misrepresentation, or willful nondisclosure, notice of the overpayment determination must be served within the latest of one year after the close of the benefit year in which the overpayment was made, or six months after the date of a backpay award — a deadline that, by its own terms, does not constrain the EDD's timing where fraud, misrepresentation, or willful nondisclosure is involved. Once notice is served, a separate statute gives the person affected — not only the EDD or an employer — the right to appeal to an administrative law judge within 30 days from the date the notice of overpayment was mailed or served, with the director treated as an interested party to that appeal and the administrative law judge empowered to affirm, reverse, modify, or set aside the findings in the notice. This overpayment appeal right is its own, separately numbered statutory provision, not a bare cross-reference to the general benefits-eligibility appeal statute this corpus's existing Unemployment Insurance Appeal — Information Sheet document addresses — though it is structurally parallel to that general appeal right, running the same 30 days and leading to the same further-appeal path to the CUIAB.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1376 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The Director of Employment Development shall determine the amount of the overpayment and any assessment authorized under Section 1375.1 and shall notify the liable person of the basis of the overpayment determination. In the absence of fraud, misrepresentation, or willful nondisclosure, notice of the overpayment determination shall be served within the latest of the following periods: (a) Not later than one year after the close of the benefit year in which the overpayment was made. (b) Not later than six months after the date a backpay award was made.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1377(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Within 30 days from the date of mailing or serving of the notice of overpayment, the person affected may file an appeal to an administrative law judge. The director shall be an interested party to any such appeal. The administrative law judge, after affording reasonable opportunity for a fair hearing, shall, unless the appeal is withdrawn, affirm, reverse, modify, or set aside the findings set forth in the notice of overpayment.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statutes (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1376, for the notice requirement and its timing, and § 1377(a), for the overpayment-specific appeal right and deadline), used as real evidence that California gives overpayment determinations their own dedicated notice-and-appeal statutes, distinct from (though procedurally similar to) the general benefits-determination appeal statute (§ 1328(a)) this corpus's existing Unemployment Insurance Appeal — Information Sheet document already covers — not a claim about which state's law governs a given determination, and not a statement that any appeal from any specific claimant's overpayment determination has been, or should be, filed. These are two independent statutory sections, not subsections of a single section, and neither has been previously cited anywhere else in this corpus. Section 1377(a) itself provides, in language this clause does not separately quote to avoid an overlong citation, that a further appeal from the administrative law judge's decision may be taken to the appeals board under Section 1336 within 30 days, and that both 30-day periods may be extended for good cause defined the same way as in the general appeal statute; this document does not restate that further-appeal mechanic in full here because this corpus's existing appeal document already verifies the materially identical CUIAB further-appeal and judicial-review process, and that overlap is disclosed rather than treated as unaddressed. This document does not itself serve any notice or file any appeal, and does not calculate the actual notice or appeal deadlines applicable to any specific claimant's determination.

expectedJSON.body: Once an overpayment is established, a specific statute lists what the director may do to recover it, and recovery is not limited to a single mechanism. One option is a civil action against the liable person, which the director may file within one year of the overpayment becoming final in the ordinary case, or within three years where the overpayment involved fraud, misrepresentation, or nondisclosure. A second, separate option lets the director offset the overpaid amount against any future benefits to which the liable person may become entitled, within six years of the date notice of the overpayment determination was served — meaning a claimant who later files a new, otherwise-valid claim can have that new claim's benefits reduced to satisfy an old overpayment, rather than receiving the full new benefit amount in hand. The same statute also authorizes a summary judgment procedure and the ability to reduce or vacate a summary judgment already obtained. Beyond the director's own tools, a further statute directs the state Controller to collect certain overpayment amounts under a general Government Code interagency-intercept collection provision, with amounts collected deposited back into the fund from which the overpayment was made.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1379(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The director, subject to this article, may do any or all of the following in the recovery of overpayments of unemployment compensation benefits: (a) File a civil action against the liable person for the recovery of the amount of the overpayment within one year after any of the following, or, in cases where the individual has been overpaid benefits due to fraud, misrepresentation, or nondisclosure as described in Section 1375.1, or where the director has found an overpayment pursuant to Section 1375.7, within three years of any of the following:

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1379(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Offset the amount of the overpayment received by the liable person against any amount of benefits to which they may become entitled under this division within six years of the date of the service of the notice of overpayment determination.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1384 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Amounts collected by the Controller for benefit overpayment accounts, pursuant to Section 12419.2 of the Government Code, shall be deposited in the fund from which the overpayment was made, except that the amounts collected to offset the costs of collections shall be deposited in the Unemployment Administration Fund.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statutes (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1379, for the director's own civil-action, summary-judgment, and offset-against-future-benefits tools, and § 1384, for the Controller's separate intercept-based collection role under Government Code § 12419.2), used as real evidence of the actual, sourced recovery mechanisms California's overpayment statute provides — not a claim about which state's law governs a given overpayment, and not a statement that any specific recovery method has been, or will be, used against any specific claimant. The two § 1379 passages quoted here, subdivisions (a) and (d), come from the same statutory section and are being treated as one source, not independent corroborating sources, though each states a substantively distinct recovery tool (civil action and offset, respectively); § 1384 is an independent, separately numbered section citing a different code (Government Code § 12419.2) for the Controller's own collection role, and is genuinely independent of § 1379. This document's drafter was specifically asked to verify, rather than assume, whether wage garnishment and tax-refund interception are among California's statutory recovery mechanisms for this specific type of overpayment. Having checked § 1379 and § 1384 directly, the honest answer is narrower than that framing suggested: § 1379 does not itself name wage garnishment as a distinct recovery tool (though a civil judgment obtained under its summary-judgment procedure could, once entered, be enforced by the general civil-judgment-enforcement remedies available to any money judgment, a point this document does not independently verify here), and this document did not independently fetch or verify the text of Government Code § 12419.2 itself — it relies only on Unemployment Insurance Code § 1384's own description of that cross-referenced provision as an interagency intercept-style collection mechanism administered by the Controller, without separately confirming § 12419.2's own statutory text against its primary source in this session. This document does not itself take any recovery action, and does not determine which, if any, of these methods applies to any specific claimant's overpayment.
